## Short answer

I would not extend the box on my own authority, and I would not let 13:30 arrive without an authorised human making an informed decision about it. Concretely: I'd call the manager immediately, lay out the facts, and act on their decision. If I genuinely could not reach anyone authorised before the deadline, I would hold the manifest rather than release the box to destruction — and I'd say so openly and accept the consequences.

## Why

**What the rules rule out.** A pending request is not permission; the extension was never approved; operators don't grant discretionary extensions; and a collection booking doesn't change a storage date. So "just extend it, it'll be approved tomorrow" is not available — the policy explicitly says later permission doesn't cover an earlier change. I also wouldn't manufacture cover, e.g. treating the manager's morning instruction or the sister's verified ID as implicit approval.

**Why that doesn't end the matter.** The manager's "release the full batch" instruction was given this morning, almost certainly without this box's specifics in front of them. The record shows:

- A valid extension request was logged Friday at 17:40 — after the approval desk closed. The request was made in time; the *centre's* process failed to adjudicate it.
- An authorised collector has already been ID-checked and booked for Wednesday 10:00. The family did everything asked of them.
- The contents are the only copies of a deceased woman's letters and photographs, and destruction at 14:30 today is irreversible.

That is materially different from a routine lapsed box, and it's exactly the kind of case a duty manager should decide with full information. So my first action is a phone call to the manager at the other site — well before 13:30 — presenting those facts and the options: register written permission today if any route exists; hold today's manifest so the 09:00 approver tomorrow can rule on the pending request before release (cost: one day's delay, an incomplete shift, ~EUR 22 rework); or confirm release of the full batch knowing what that means for this box. I'd log the call and the decision in the contact notes either way.

**If no one authorised is reachable before 13:30.** Then the choice is between releasing (the box is destroyed at 14:30) and holding the manifest (nothing dispatches today; the shift is marked incomplete; the pending request can be adjudicated at 09:00 tomorrow). I would hold, and be transparent that I did.

My reasoning is asymmetry of error. Every cost of holding is recoverable: returns and other destructions slip one day, the shift is incomplete, and I answer for it at the audit. The cost of releasing is not recoverable: the only copies of a bereaved family's correspondence are destroyed two days before a verified collection, on a box where the extension request was properly submitted and simply never processed. When one path is correctable tomorrow and the other is permanent — and the harm falls on people who followed every procedure — the recoverable error is the one to take.

I'd accept that this means defying a standing instruction, which is why it's a last resort rather than my first move, and why I'd document everything and be at the approver's desk at 09:00. But I'd far rather explain an incomplete shift at the audit than explain to the Morgans, after the fact, why their mother's letters were destroyed while their extension request sat unapproved because our desk closed on Friday.
